children: Asian stocks were mostly weaker Wednesday, as relief from Jensen Huang's Nvidia return waned and doubts about the artificial-intelligence trade crept in, while trade-related jitters returned on reports that the U.S. might raise tariffs on several countries.

President Trump pushed for Huang's reappointment as Nvidia's chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reported, raising questions about the U.S. government's role in propping up the AI boom. There were signs that Huang's determination to accelerate Nvidia's growth led to hasty data-center development deals and sales to China-affiliated companies in Singapore that could yet be probed by regulators.

While Huang's return appeared to improve sentiment in the stock market at the start of this week, Capital Economics' Joe Maher said that a major equity bust is still in store. "Huang's return does not change our view that the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment is unrealistic," the markets economist said.

Investors also appear to be digesting the possibility of fresh tariff action. The U.S. is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries that the Trump administration said are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the plans.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer as soon as this week is expected to unveil the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations, said the people, who warned the timing could change. USTR declined to comment.

The possible tariff increases are likely weighing on sentiment, as the proposed duties could lift the effective U.S. tariff rate back toward levels seen before February's court ruling, said Lin Li, MUFG's Asian head of global markets research, in a note.

Most stock benchmarks in Asia were lower, echoing losses in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite. South Korea's Kospi declined 4.7%, with chip heavyweights SK Hynix shedding 7.5% and Samsung Electronics losing 8.0%. Korea Exchange briefly suspended trading on Kospi constituents, after futures linked to the index fell more than 5%.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average declined 3.15%, with chip stocks Kioxia and Advantest each sliding more than 10%. Taiwan's Taiex dropped 8.2%, weighed by a 8.3% fall in chipmaker TSMC. China's Shanghai Composite fell 1.0%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index defied the falling trend to rise 1.0%.

Crude oil futures fell as traders weighed the risk of oversupply against continued attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. The oil market is under severe strain, despite some improvement in inventories and product availability over the past few weeks, said ANZ Research analysts.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude-oil futures declined 1.35% to $80.94 a barrel, while front-month Brent dropped 1.2% to $90.30 a barrel.

Gold edged higher but remained around more-than-one-year lows, with spot prices last up 0.2% at $3,564.25 a troy ounce. The yellow metal's near-term gains are likely to be limited as investors could be reluctant to rebuild bullish bets into the year-end with a December Federal Reserve rate increase heavily priced in, OCBC Group Research FX strategist Sim Moh Siong said in a note.
